text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, behavioural activation, a simpler, cheaper form of
psychotherapy for depression. How to make our healthcare system, especially
our hospitals, safer. Could Victoria show us the way after a disaster in one of
their maternity services?

And, cervical cancer. Cancer in the neck of the uterus is a nasty malignancy
which is harder to treat. But luckily it's preventable by screening. For many years
Australia has been a world leader in cervical cancer screening using the so-
called Pap smear, looking for rogue cells under the microscope. The result has
been very low rates of invasive cervical cancer by international standards. But
from next year cervical cancer screening will undergo a radical change, and
some have asked whether it will be safe.

A paper in this morning's Medical Journal of Australia has tried to answer that
question, and one of the authors, Karen Canfell of the Cancer Council New
South Wales is in the studio with us, as is Jonathan Carter, director of
gynaecological oncology at the Chris O'Brien Lifehouse Cancer Centre in
Sydney. Welcome to the Health Report, both of you.

Jonathan, what are the changes from next year?

Jonathan Carter: Well, up until now the Pap smear screening system, which
originated back in the 1990s as a national and coordinated approach, involved
Pap smears for women aged from 18 onwards every two years. And whilst that
has been a great step forward with a reduction in the incidence of about 50% in
patients developing cervical cancers, that incidence has plateaued over recent
years. And so the current recommendations which will be coming into effect in
May of next year involves a test called the HPV test, which is kind of like from the
Pap test, it's not a blood test…

Norman Swan: So you're scraping the cervix as well?

Jonathan Carter: So the women will still need to have a scrape of the cervix, but
instead of having a smear performed, the laboratories will look for the DNA of the
HPV virus, which we now know is the causative agent for cervical cancer. So
every five years women will be invited to have an HPV test.
 
Norman Swan: From the age of 25.

Jonathan Carter: From the age of 25. And if that HPV test is positive, they will
have a reflex smear and colposcopy.

Norman Swan: And so the difference, apart from the HPV testing, so it's every
five years, and it's by invitation. So at the moment, unless you got a really good
GP who has a system for recall, it's up to the woman to actually remember to go
along to have her smear.

Jonathan Carter: Yes, that's correct.

Norman Swan: So the worry is younger women, maybe you're neglecting
younger women. There's the issue of interval cancers, if it's every five years are
you going to develop cancer in between times. And it's the younger women,
Karen, that you've been looking at in the study in this week's Medical Journal of
Australia. Tell us about the study.

Karen Canfell: That's right, Norman. So what we've done is on the threshold of
these major changes we've done a 25-year look-back essentially. So we looked
at the performance of the national cervical screening program in women of
different ages over the time since the program was initiated…

Norman Swan: So it's 1988 or something like that.

Karen Canfell: Yes, from the late '80s, the program was initiated in '91, and we
looked at the performance of the program over 20 years.

Norman Swan: And just by way of background, we've probably been over-
testing even by Pap smear standards, because Finland has been doing once
every three years for a long time and they've got lower rates than us.

Karen Canfell: Well, that's right, and in fact the international recommendations
are to screen only every three years in younger women with Pap smears and to
start at age 25 even with Pap smears.

Norman Swan: When we suggested that in Australia there was World War III
with the pathologists and some gynaecologists.
 
Karen Canfell: Well, I think what has changed is a couple of things. First of all,
the emergence of major international evidence on the greater effectiveness of
HPV DNA testing. It's a much more sensitive test. And secondly the impact of the
HPV vaccine which has been huge, and we've seen this collapse of HPV
infections in younger women.

Norman Swan: So when you analyse the data by age group over the last nearly
30 years, what did you find?

Karen Canfell: So we found that there has been this great reduction of 50% or
more in women over the age of 25, and in fact that reduction holds over beyond
the age of stopping screening. So we found this similar reduction even in women
over the age of 70 who aren't targeted by the screening program. So that's
fantastic. It shows that there is long-term hold-over benefits from regular
screening. We found that there were no changes in rates in younger women
under the age of 25.

Norman Swan: So screening made no difference to them?

Karen Canfell: Screening made no difference over the 20-year period.

Norman Swan: Well, the good news in that is that starting at 25 is not going to
make any difference in theory. But why is it not making any impact?

Karen Canfell: Well, the new program, first of all to say it's predicted to be 20%
even more effective than the current program, so there's that…

Norman Swan: Okay, that's the PR, but let's go to…I'm being cynical, but just tell
me why under the 25 it had no impact. Is that a different kind of cancer or…?

Karen Canfell: Well, there's a few reasons and it is consistent with a lot of
international evidence. First of all, cervical cancer is very, very rare in that age
group. Secondly, we have a lot of evidence that the testing doesn't pick it up well.
It may be that there is a rare subtype of cancer that is more aggressive, but we
have a lot of data now that shows that screening makes no impact in that age
group, and I think the new study today just confirms that in the Australian context.
 
Norman Swan: So Jonathan, this is in the context of this group of younger
women are largely going to be immunised against HPV coming through, so it's
not a completely naive group. The other finding…

Jonathan Carter: Well, they will be immunised currently with a four valent or…

Norman Swan: So not against every HPV…

Jonathan Carter: No. So the current vaccine is only effective against 70% of the
HPV genotypes or strains. There is another vaccine that has been released in
the United States which has nine strains which covers about 90% of the…

Norman Swan: So there's still a risk, even if you've been immunised.

Jonathan Carter: Well, women who have been vaccinated still require to be
screened.

Norman Swan: What about interval cancers? Because you can get them in
mammographic screening for breast cancer. You know, you have your
mammographic screening and then a cancer appears before your next screen. In
five years are you likely to…?

Jonathan Carter: Look, it's a very uncommon, extraordinarily rare for there to be
a rapidly progressing cervical cancer. And greater than 99% of all cervical
cancers contain HPV virus. So if a woman is HPV negative, the risk for having
precancer is extraordinarily low, and then developing cancer after that,
remembering there is a large time between contracting the virus to developing
persistence, precancer and then cancer. So even going from precancer to
cancer, that is estimated to take 7 to 10 years.

Norman Swan: And what about interval cancer in your study?

Karen Canfell: So we just looked at cancer outcomes, but we've got a lot of
international evidence now that HPV screening protects for a long time. And in
fact some countries are going to 10-yearly intervals in older women.

Norman Swan: The other thing you discovered will in this study was…there are
a few different types of cervical cancers, not just one type, and there's another
type, the one we are talking about mostly is called squamous cell carcinoma, and
 
there's another one called adenocarcinoma…it doesn't really matter what the
names are. Screening has not affected adenocarcinoma at all. And I'm just
wondering from either of you is HPV…they are both affected by HPV, is HPV
testing going to affect adenocarcinoma?

Karen Canfell: Yes, that's our prediction, because 80% or more, in fact even
more than squamous cells cancers are caused by the HPV virus. So HPV testing
and HPV vaccination is predicted to impact these in a much more cognisant way
than the Pap smear screening program has been able to.

Norman Swan: And is that because the adenocarcinoma is more inside the
cervix and the scrape doesn't pick it up?

Jonathan Carter: Well, there's a number of different reasons, Norman. The Pap
smear wasn't a great test. A good test is not a great test, so it's not as accurate
as some people think. It is scraping the cervix on the outside of the cervix where
the squamous lesions are and it's less reliable, everybody knows that, in picking
up the glandular lesions which are on the inside of the cervix. So yes, there are
lesions within the cervix that may not be reached by a standard Pap smear. And
the Pap smear itself, its accuracy is…we talk about sensitivity and specificity, as
you know, is in the order of 60% to 70%.

Norman Swan: So you can miss a cancer when it's there.

Jonathan Carter: Absolutely.

Norman Swan: And are we going for…we have over-tested women for cervical
cancer in the past, I think that's a reasonable thing to say according to the
evidence, are we still over-testing? Could you get away with once every 10 years
for HPV testing? Are we being super careful here?

Jonathan Carter: I don't think there's anything wrong with being super careful,
and it's a big step from two-yearly to five-yearly screening. I think, like everything
that has been done up until now and with the current guidelines, it should be
evidence-based in our climate.

Norman Swan: So participation rates, Karen, in colorectal cancer screening are
pathetic in Australia, they are down about 32%, 33%, in Victoria maybe about
 
36%, and that's probably the best in the country. And one argument…there are
two arguments for why it's not very good, one is people don't like the idea of
rubbing their poo on a test, but equally women don't particularly like having their
Pap smear done, so that's one comparison. And the other issue is that the
federal government made a mistake in taking control of the colorectal cancer
program, where cervical cancer is under the control of GPs and they have made
sure it works. By making it by invitation, are you taking control away from GPs
who some would argue are at the heart of the success of a cervical cancer
screening program?

Karen Canfell: So we are certainly not taking control away from GPs, Norman,
but the biggest change at the moment is that we will send a proactive invitation to
the woman to screen on her 25th birthday, and then proactive invitations every
five years thereafter. So certainly that doesn't take away from the GPs
management, but it really means that we will have a good central system in place
for reminding women.

Jonathan Carter: I agree, absolutely.

Norman Swan: And the role of gynaecologists? Because gynaecologists have
been…you go and see your gynaecologist for a check-up rather than your GP,
and gynaecologists like to do the Pap smear. What is the role of the
gynaecologist in all this?

Jonathan Carter: Look, I think the majority of Pap smears can, should and are
currently being done by general practitioners, family practitioners, and that's
where most are done. When the smear is abnormal, the HPV test is abnormal,
that's when gynaecologists are involved.

Norman Swan: And is there any benefit at all for a woman who has missed out
on HPV testing in adolescence being HPV immunised…

Jonathan Carter: HPV vaccinated.

Norman Swan: Sorry, she has not been HPV vaccinated, she gets her first test
at 25 and she is HPV negative. Should she be vaccinated?
 
Karen Canfell: She should be screened. So the thing about vaccination is it's
most effective when it is given to preadolescents. So that's why the program has
traditionally targeted the youngest 12- to 13-year-olds with a catch-up initially.
But the thing that we really want to say is that vaccination and screening have to
work together. So whether vaccinated or not, the woman should be…

Norman Swan: You haven't answered my question. She is HPV negative, why
shouldn't she be immunised?

Jonathan Carter: It's a very complex issue, and the HPV test is based upon cells
that are scraped from the cervix. The relationship between that and her immune
system having developed a natural immune response is poor. 50% of people
who are infected actually don't have an immune response. So if she is going to
be continually exposed to HPV, then she may derive some benefit from being
vaccinated.

Norman Swan: But it doesn't really tell her true HPV status in terms of her
exposure through life?

Jonathan Carter: It will tell her what is going on in the cells on her cervix, which
is where the malignant transformation will take place. It won't tell her what her
immune status is.

Karen Canfell: So the beauty of the move to HPV screening is that in fact it
doesn't matter what a woman's past vaccination status is, we will be able to
basically assess her risk based on the HPV result that we find.

Norman Swan: Thanks very much to you both, to Karen Canfell who is director
of the Cancer Research Division, Cancer Council New South Wales, and
Jonathan Carter who is director of Gynaecological Oncology at the Chris O'Brien
the Lifehouse Cancer Centre. Thanks very much to you both.

You're listening to the Health Report here on RN, ABC news radio and CBC radio
across Canada.

Perhaps one in 10 people in Australian hospitals suffer a complication, and half
of those are avoidable. What we're talking about is anything from wound
infections, to bone fractures, to bedsores, to drug side-effects, to death. Victoria
 
has been in the spotlight because of seven preventable deaths of babies in its
Djerriwarrh maternity service, and are finding that the Victorian Health
Department's processes were unable to detect problems with what's called
clinical governance where standards of care in a hospital were not being
monitored or acted upon appropriately perhaps. Hence a review of the safety and
quality system in Victoria which has been released in the last few days. It's called
Targeting Zero, and it was chaired by Professor Stephen Duckett at the Grattan
Institute who is in our Melbourne studio. Welcome Stephen.

Stephen Duckett: Good evening, Norman.

Norman Swan: So you did this review, it wasn't of the Djerriwarrh service
because that's already been done by the Safety and Quality Council and
Professor Euan Wallace. You were looking at the system in general.

Stephen Duckett: Yes, we were looking more broadly. Obviously the report was
stimulated, the inquiry was stimulated by the Djerriwarrh health service tragedy.
But we were looking at the overall system and the governance of the whole
system.

Norman Swan: And just to get the sense of this right, we are not…when things
go wrong, it's not usually because of a bad egg, is because the system goes
wrong. So we are not looking for a head on a stick here.

Stephen Duckett: No, there are quite separate processes, including the
Australian Health Professional Registration Authority that looks at those bad egg
issues. We were looking at the overall system governance, the processes, the
information and that sort of thing.

Norman Swan: So you weren't that kind to the Victorian Health Department.

Stephen Duckett: Well, we were quite strong in our language. There were these
11 potentially avoidable deaths, and this is a tragedy, and I would like to see that
we learnt from that.

Norman Swan: So what do you think the main learnings are from your review?

Stephen Duckett: Victoria is right at the forefront of being well regarded as the
most efficient state in terms of public hospital provision. But other states have
 
jumped ahead of Victoria in terms of quality and safety governance. New South
Wales has a much better infrastructure for governance of quality and safety
following the Garling Report I think a decade or so ago. Queensland, much better
systems of tracking and monitoring safety issues following the Patel Bundaberg
tragedy. South Australia, a better incident reporting system. So other states are
going ahead, and Victoria hasn't kept up with them.

Norman Swan: So what sort of changes are you suggesting?

Stephen Duckett: Well, we've got a number of them, there's 180 almost
recommendations. But some of them are these things where we want more
clinical engagement. The department wasn't using the skills, knowledge of
clinicians as much as it ought. We want more transparency, we want to be
publishing how hospitals are going, public and private in terms of their safety and
quality performance. And we want to have the health department being more
supportive of health services and providing advice. At the moment every single
hospital has to reinvent the safety and quality wheel, and there's not as much
sharing of knowledge and transmission of knowledge about what works across
the health system.

Norman Swan: Despite Victoria being proud of its system and its decentralised
approach, it is unique in that I think there are something like 85 different health
services in Victoria, whereas in New South Wales it might be…I don't know what
it is, 17, similar sort of number in Queensland. So they've shrunk it down from
bigger services. And I think one of your findings was that in Victoria you've got
some very small services which don't really have the skills to look after
themselves properly in terms of safety and quality.

Stephen Duckett: Yes, so we have proposed strengthening the boards. At the
moment some of these boards have been in place…the members have been on
them for 20 or 30 years, and so there's no turnover, no new ideas coming
through. There is not an adequate process for ensuring that they've got the right
skills. At the moment there is a tick box; do you have clinical governance skills or
not. Who knows what that means? And so we are proposing major strengthening
of the board level clinical governance because they are the ones that are legally
accountable.
 
Norman Swan: Let's talk about clinical governance because the average listener
listening to us now wouldn't have a clue what we are talking about. We are
talking about clinicians sitting around a table trying to look at events that might
have occurred in the hospital, then doing research into why that would happen so
it doesn't happen again. And just anecdotally, it depends on rather honest
conversations occurring which probably don't really occur. So you're talking
about engaging doctors more in this, but they are actually traditionally quite
scared to bring this up with their colleagues, even people who you would think
are just big bruiser orthopaedic surgeons and would be scared of anything, but
there are actually scared of raising stuff with their colleagues.

Stephen Duckett: Yes, there are two paths we are really talking about. One is
these events, the unusual, the sentinel events, as they're called, operating on the
wrong body part or leaving something in the wound. They are very unusual, and
they are investigated to death, in a sense. What we also need to be looking at is
patterns of care. To what extent are there more hospital-acquired infections in
your hospital, in your clinical unit, in your orthopaedic unit than in the state
average. And unfortunately what has happened in Victoria is the hospitals
themselves don't have enough information about what the state average is, they
even don't have good information about how they are tracking against their own
history. So by focusing on patterns, you…I won't say make the person irrelevant,
but it gets you to focus more on the systems, it gets you to focus on are there
systematic things happening in this hospital that aren't happening in other
hospitals.

Norman Swan: You also say in your report, which would shock the average
person, is that safety and quality doesn't have a high enough profile, either at a
state level or at a hospital level.

Stephen Duckett: Yes, as I said, Victoria is very proud of the fact that it's the
most efficient state in terms of the public hospital system, and they've
strengthened their emphasis on safety and quality in recent years. But the
example I use is there's a performance assessment scale that is used to rank
hospitals, to track how they are going. And at the moment there are three
dimensions to it. Are you going on budget? And that's worth 30% of the score…
 
Norman Swan: And the second one is are you going on budget, and the third
one is are you going on budget, is it?

Stephen Duckett: Not quite as bad as that, Norman! But the first one is are you
going on budget, the second one is how are you going on your waiting list, and
the third one is quality and safety. Originally that was only 15%, and they have
increased that to 40%.

But when I wait around Victoria and said to people; do you think it's the right idea
that if you go better on budget you are allowed to go worse on quality and
safety? I couldn't find anybody who thought that was a good idea at all. So quality
and safety…

Norman Swan: It's got to sit there in its own right.

Stephen Duckett: Yes, it ought to be there in its own right, it ought to be
something that we focus on, and it's not at the moment.

Norman Swan: But to do this you can't expect a single service, even a large
service like, say, Royal Melbourne or the Alfred, you can't expect them to do a lot
of this stuff by themselves. The department is going to have to do a lot for them,
aren't they?

Stephen Duckett: Yes, exactly. So what we are saying is there needs to be way
more support from the Department to these services, and so for example in New
South Wales there is a portal that clinicians across the state can access which
provides them with information about how they are tracking against their peers,
how they are tracking against the state average. We don't have that in Victoria.
And so we need to be providing more support to the clinicians in our hospitals,
big and small, to help them address these important issues.

Norman Swan: When there was a problem in Britain in a hospital in Staffordshire
in the Midlands, the big question in the National Health Service was how many
more Staffordshires are there. Do we know how many more Djerriwarrhs there
are in Victoria or indeed any other state in Australia?

Stephen Duckett: I think some states are better than others in tracking what's
going wrong, and in trying to identify the issues. When I was in Queensland, this
 
was one of the things…we wanted to err on identifying things early. And so we
probably over-investigated, just to make sure that Bundaberg would never
happen again, or reduce to a small risk that Bundaberg happen again. We
haven't had that same focus in Victoria, and I think that's what we need.

Norman Swan: And just finally Stephen, how much can other states learn
from…you say that other states are ahead of Victoria in some respects, but how
much is this applicable to other states?

Stephen Duckett: There are some national issues that we raise. So, for
example, there needs to be better sharing of information between the registration
regulation bodies and the health services, because we know that if a person, a
doctor for example, has complaints against him or her, they are more likely to
have complaints against them in the future. But we don't get that information, it's
secret squirrel business in the regulator. And so we need to have much more
sharing of information. So there are some national issues that we touch on in that
report.

Norman Swan: Thanks very much Stephen, and that's available on the Health
Department's website?

Stephen Duckett: On the Health Department website. Thanks very much
Norman.

Norman Swan: Stephen Duckett, who is head of the health program at the
Grattan Institute in Melbourne.

You're listening to the Health Report here on RN with me, Norman Swan.

There is a form of treatment for depression called behavioural activation. There's
just been a fascinating trial published in the Lancet comparing it to the standard
psychotherapy for depression called cognitive behavioural therapy. And one of
the authors of this trial is David Ekers from the University of Durham. Welcome to
the Health Report.

David Ekers: Hiya Norman.

Norman Swan: What is behavioural activation?
 
David Ekers: Behavioural activation, it's not a new treatment for depression, it's
been around a long time, and it has a view that depression is not necessarily
something wrong inside us but something that has happened that has cut us off
from those things in our world that are important or antidepressant to us. And as
that happens, if it happens to any of us we would feel down, it would affect our
mood, and sometimes when people feel down, to cope they tend to put things off
or shut down, and when they shut down they become further isolated from those
things, and thus the loop develops.

So behavioural activation is a relatively simple treatment that aims at helping
people understand that relationship between what they do and how they feel, and
then look at changing what they do on a day-to-day basis, just with small gradual
steps to put them back in touch with the things in their world that are healthy and
antidepressants to them, and in that way subsequently they change how they
feel. So we call that in BA working from the outside in.

Norman Swan: So what did you used to enjoy, doing kind of an audit of things
you used to have fun with and that you are not doing now.

David Ekers: Yes, it's a little bit more complicated than just fun. It would be
lovely to think we could live a hedonistic lifestyle…

Norman Swan: Yes, particularly going to the football if your team is not winning,
yes.

David Ekers: Yes, it's things that are valuable, that give us a sense of purpose or
meaning in our day-to-day lives. Some of that will be pleasure, some of it will be
necessary tasks, some of it will be things like going to work or communicating
with family members. Not all of it is pleasurable but it's functional for us. So BA is
a contextual treatment, it looks at depression as sat in the context of your life.

Norman Swan: So I take it that the activation piece is not 'get up off your arse
and stop feeling sorry to yourself'.

David Ekers: No, not at all. What BA does is first of all it explores that concept
with people. So it develops…

Norman Swan: So you understand what the meaning of those activities were.
 
David Ekers: Yes, and then you understand how they have gone out of your life.
Because they go out of your life often for a reason. Things will have happened
that will make it difficult to do those things, so we explore that with somebody,
then we get them to look at the relationship at the moment between what they
are doing and how they're feeling, and then we gradually work together to
develop a plan, a thing called activity scheduling, to put people back in touch with
that stuff. And then you regularly monitor that and you look at blocks in that
treatment and work out what people can do to get out of…

Norman Swan: So there's a bit of cognitive stuff in there as well. You might
think, well, I can't go and do that because everybody knows I've been depressed
and they're going to think that I'm weak and hopeless. And you've got to get
beyond that negative thought as well.

David Ekers: Yes, but it's fundamentally different to cognitive behavioural
therapy. So in behavioural activation what we do is we are more interested in the
consequence of thinking that way. So we will recognise how people ruminate and
think about things, we all do that and it's much, much worse if we are
experiencing depression. We get less into trying to challenge the meaning of that
for an individual, which is how cognitive behavioural therapy works, and we are
much more interested in the consequence of that. So when you started feeling
that way, what did you do? And when you did that, how did you feel? And was
that in the longer term more beneficial? In the short term people do things to take
away the stress, but in the longer term we look at how that keeps people where
they are.

Norman Swan: I spent so long talking about behavioural activation, I'm almost
running out of time here to talk about your trial, but essentially you did a semi-
randomised trial of comparing behavioural activation with quite inexperienced
therapists, in other words, they weren't PhDs in psychology, versus a course of
cognitive behavioural therapy. What did you find?

David Ekers: Well, it was a randomised trial, it was a completely randomised
trial. Participants were randomised completely at random away from the
control…
 
Norman Swan: Oh I thought you selected people to make sure that you had a
balanced set of…

David Ekers: No, we made sure each group were balanced on a few things,
which is good quality randomised controlled trial. And what we found was non-
inferiority. So we found that BA delivered by non-specialists was not inferior in
any way to the current goal standard of CBT delivered by therapists…

Norman Swan: So does non-inferior mean just as good as?

David Ekers: Well, not quite. What you do is you set an inferiority margin around
on a measure and you would plan to get your new treatment, the BA, within that
margin of the gold standard, because to prove something is exactly the same
you'd need an unfeasibly large study to do that.

Norman Swan: And you found it was also significantly cheaper?

David Ekers: Yes, we got about a 20% reduction in costs. So I think what is
interesting in this study, the National Institute for Clinical Excellence over here
asked for this study to be done, but what's really interesting is what we've shown
is that a very effective psychological treatment can be delivered by non-
specialists to the same standards as specialists. And when we have difficulty in
access to psychological treatments, which I think is worldwide, this could offer
some promise.

Norman Swan: Dr David Ekers, who is clinical senior lecturer in the School of
Medicine, Pharmacy and Health in Durham University in the UK.

I'm Norman Swan, this has been the Health Report, and I'll see you next week.

pages.text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to this week's Health Report with me,
Norman Swan. Today, behavioural activation, a simpler, cheaper form of
psychotherapy for depression. How to make our healthcare system, especially
our hospitals, safer. Could Victoria show us the way after a disaster in one of
their maternity services?

And, cervical cancer. Cancer in the neck of the uterus is a nasty malignancy
which is harder to treat. But luckily it's preventable by screening. For many years
Australia has been a world leader in cervical cancer screening using the so-
called Pap smear, looking for rogue cells under the microscope. The result has
been very low rates of invasive cervical cancer by international standards. But
from next year cervical cancer screening will undergo a radical change, and
some have asked whether it will be safe.

A paper in this morning's Medical Journal of Australia has tried to answer that
question, and one of the authors, Karen Canfell of the Cancer Council New
South Wales is in the studio with us, as is Jonathan Carter, director of
gynaecological oncology at the Chris O'Brien Lifehouse Cancer Centre in
Sydney. Welcome to the Health Report, both of you.

Jonathan, what are the changes from next year?

Jonathan Carter: Well, up until now the Pap smear screening system, which
originated back in the 1990s as a national and coordinated approach, involved
Pap smears for women aged from 18 onwards every two years. And whilst that
has been a great step forward with a reduction in the incidence of about 50% in
patients developing cervical cancers, that incidence has plateaued over recent
years. And so the current recommendations which will be coming into effect in
May of next year involves a test called the HPV test, which is kind of like from the
Pap test, it's not a blood test…

Norman Swan: So you're scraping the cervix as well?

Jonathan Carter: So the women will still need to have a scrape of the cervix, but
instead of having a smear performed, the laboratories will look for the DNA of the
HPV virus, which we now know is the causative agent for cervical cancer. So
every five years women will be invited to have an HPV test.

Norman Swan: From the age of 25.

Jonathan Carter: From the age of 25. And if that HPV test is positive, they will
have a reflex smear and colposcopy.

Norman Swan: And so the difference, apart from the HPV testing, so it's every
five years, and it's by invitation. So at the moment, unless you got a really good
GP who has a system for recall, it's up to the woman to actually remember to go
along to have her smear.

Jonathan Carter: Yes, that's correct.

Norman Swan: So the worry is younger women, maybe you're neglecting
younger women. There's the issue of interval cancers, if it's every five years are
you going to develop cancer in between times. And it's the younger women,
Karen, that you've been looking at in the study in this week's Medical Journal of
Australia. Tell us about the study.

Karen Canfell: That's right, Norman. So what we've done is on the threshold of
these major changes we've done a 25-year look-back essentially. So we looked
at the performance of the national cervical screening program in women of
different ages over the time since the program was initiated…

Norman Swan: So it's 1988 or something like that.

Karen Canfell: Yes, from the late '80s, the program was initiated in '91, and we
looked at the performance of the program over 20 years.

Norman Swan: And just by way of background, we've probably been over-
testing even by Pap smear standards, because Finland has been doing once
every three years for a long time and they've got lower rates than us.

Karen Canfell: Well, that's right, and in fact the international recommendations
are to screen only every three years in younger women with Pap smears and to
start at age 25 even with Pap smears.

Norman Swan: When we suggested that in Australia there was World War III
with the pathologists and some gynaecologists.

Karen Canfell: Well, I think what has changed is a couple of things. First of all,
the emergence of major international evidence on the greater effectiveness of
HPV DNA testing. It's a much more sensitive test. And secondly the impact of the
HPV vaccine which has been huge, and we've seen this collapse of HPV
infections in younger women.

Norman Swan: So when you analyse the data by age group over the last nearly
30 years, what did you find?

Karen Canfell: So we found that there has been this great reduction of 50% or
more in women over the age of 25, and in fact that reduction holds over beyond
the age of stopping screening. So we found this similar reduction even in women
over the age of 70 who aren't targeted by the screening program. So that's
fantastic. It shows that there is long-term hold-over benefits from regular
screening. We found that there were no changes in rates in younger women
under the age of 25.

Norman Swan: So screening made no difference to them?

Karen Canfell: Screening made no difference over the 20-year period.

Norman Swan: Well, the good news in that is that starting at 25 is not going to
make any difference in theory. But why is it not making any impact?

Karen Canfell: Well, the new program, first of all to say it's predicted to be 20%
even more effective than the current program, so there's that…

Norman Swan: Okay, that's the PR, but let's go to…I'm being cynical, but just tell
me why under the 25 it had no impact. Is that a different kind of cancer or…?

Karen Canfell: Well, there's a few reasons and it is consistent with a lot of
international evidence. First of all, cervical cancer is very, very rare in that age
group. Secondly, we have a lot of evidence that the testing doesn't pick it up well.
It may be that there is a rare subtype of cancer that is more aggressive, but we
have a lot of data now that shows that screening makes no impact in that age
group, and I think the new study today just confirms that in the Australian context.

Norman Swan: So Jonathan, this is in the context of this group of younger
women are largely going to be immunised against HPV coming through, so it's
not a completely naive group. The other finding…

Jonathan Carter: Well, they will be immunised currently with a four valent or…

Norman Swan: So not against every HPV…

Jonathan Carter: No. So the current vaccine is only effective against 70% of the
HPV genotypes or strains. There is another vaccine that has been released in
the United States which has nine strains which covers about 90% of the…

Norman Swan: So there's still a risk, even if you've been immunised.

Jonathan Carter: Well, women who have been vaccinated still require to be
screened.

Norman Swan: What about interval cancers? Because you can get them in
mammographic screening for breast cancer. You know, you have your
mammographic screening and then a cancer appears before your next screen. In
five years are you likely to…?

Jonathan Carter: Look, it's a very uncommon, extraordinarily rare for there to be
a rapidly progressing cervical cancer. And greater than 99% of all cervical
cancers contain HPV virus. So if a woman is HPV negative, the risk for having
precancer is extraordinarily low, and then developing cancer after that,
remembering there is a large time between contracting the virus to developing
persistence, precancer and then cancer. So even going from precancer to
cancer, that is estimated to take 7 to 10 years.

Norman Swan: And what about interval cancer in your study?

Karen Canfell: So we just looked at cancer outcomes, but we've got a lot of
international evidence now that HPV screening protects for a long time. And in
fact some countries are going to 10-yearly intervals in older women.

Norman Swan: The other thing you discovered will in this study was…there are
a few different types of cervical cancers, not just one type, and there's another
type, the one we are talking about mostly is called squamous cell carcinoma, and

there's another one called adenocarcinoma…it doesn't really matter what the
names are. Screening has not affected adenocarcinoma at all. And I'm just
wondering from either of you is HPV…they are both affected by HPV, is HPV
testing going to affect adenocarcinoma?

Karen Canfell: Yes, that's our prediction, because 80% or more, in fact even
more than squamous cells cancers are caused by the HPV virus. So HPV testing
and HPV vaccination is predicted to impact these in a much more cognisant way
than the Pap smear screening program has been able to.

Norman Swan: And is that because the adenocarcinoma is more inside the
cervix and the scrape doesn't pick it up?

Jonathan Carter: Well, there's a number of different reasons, Norman. The Pap
smear wasn't a great test. A good test is not a great test, so it's not as accurate
as some people think. It is scraping the cervix on the outside of the cervix where
the squamous lesions are and it's less reliable, everybody knows that, in picking
up the glandular lesions which are on the inside of the cervix. So yes, there are
lesions within the cervix that may not be reached by a standard Pap smear. And
the Pap smear itself, its accuracy is…we talk about sensitivity and specificity, as
you know, is in the order of 60% to 70%.

Norman Swan: So you can miss a cancer when it's there.

Jonathan Carter: Absolutely.

Norman Swan: And are we going for…we have over-tested women for cervical
cancer in the past, I think that's a reasonable thing to say according to the
evidence, are we still over-testing? Could you get away with once every 10 years
for HPV testing? Are we being super careful here?

Jonathan Carter: I don't think there's anything wrong with being super careful,
and it's a big step from two-yearly to five-yearly screening. I think, like everything
that has been done up until now and with the current guidelines, it should be
evidence-based in our climate.

Norman Swan: So participation rates, Karen, in colorectal cancer screening are
pathetic in Australia, they are down about 32%, 33%, in Victoria maybe about

36%, and that's probably the best in the country. And one argument…there are
two arguments for why it's not very good, one is people don't like the idea of
rubbing their poo on a test, but equally women don't particularly like having their
Pap smear done, so that's one comparison. And the other issue is that the
federal government made a mistake in taking control of the colorectal cancer
program, where cervical cancer is under the control of GPs and they have made
sure it works. By making it by invitation, are you taking control away from GPs
who some would argue are at the heart of the success of a cervical cancer
screening program?

Karen Canfell: So we are certainly not taking control away from GPs, Norman,
but the biggest change at the moment is that we will send a proactive invitation to
the woman to screen on her 25th birthday, and then proactive invitations every
five years thereafter. So certainly that doesn't take away from the GPs
management, but it really means that we will have a good central system in place
for reminding women.

Jonathan Carter: I agree, absolutely.

Norman Swan: And the role of gynaecologists? Because gynaecologists have
been…you go and see your gynaecologist for a check-up rather than your GP,
and gynaecologists like to do the Pap smear. What is the role of the
gynaecologist in all this?

Jonathan Carter: Look, I think the majority of Pap smears can, should and are
currently being done by general practitioners, family practitioners, and that's
where most are done. When the smear is abnormal, the HPV test is abnormal,
that's when gynaecologists are involved.

Norman Swan: And is there any benefit at all for a woman who has missed out
on HPV testing in adolescence being HPV immunised…

Jonathan Carter: HPV vaccinated.

Norman Swan: Sorry, she has not been HPV vaccinated, she gets her first test
at 25 and she is HPV negative. Should she be vaccinated?

Karen Canfell: She should be screened. So the thing about vaccination is it's
most effective when it is given to preadolescents. So that's why the program has
traditionally targeted the youngest 12- to 13-year-olds with a catch-up initially.
But the thing that we really want to say is that vaccination and screening have to
work together. So whether vaccinated or not, the woman should be…

Norman Swan: You haven't answered my question. She is HPV negative, why
shouldn't she be immunised?

Jonathan Carter: It's a very complex issue, and the HPV test is based upon cells
that are scraped from the cervix. The relationship between that and her immune
system having developed a natural immune response is poor. 50% of people
who are infected actually don't have an immune response. So if she is going to
be continually exposed to HPV, then she may derive some benefit from being
vaccinated.

Norman Swan: But it doesn't really tell her true HPV status in terms of her
exposure through life?

Jonathan Carter: It will tell her what is going on in the cells on her cervix, which
is where the malignant transformation will take place. It won't tell her what her
immune status is.

Karen Canfell: So the beauty of the move to HPV screening is that in fact it
doesn't matter what a woman's past vaccination status is, we will be able to
basically assess her risk based on the HPV result that we find.

Norman Swan: Thanks very much to you both, to Karen Canfell who is director
of the Cancer Research Division, Cancer Council New South Wales, and
Jonathan Carter who is director of Gynaecological Oncology at the Chris O'Brien
the Lifehouse Cancer Centre. Thanks very much to you both.

Perhaps one in 10 people in Australian hospitals suffer a complication, and half
of those are avoidable. What we're talking about is anything from wound
infections, to bone fractures, to bedsores, to drug side-effects, to death. Victoria

has been in the spotlight because of seven preventable deaths of babies in its
Djerriwarrh maternity service, and are finding that the Victorian Health
Department's processes were unable to detect problems with what's called
clinical governance where standards of care in a hospital were not being
monitored or acted upon appropriately perhaps. Hence a review of the safety and
quality system in Victoria which has been released in the last few days. It's called
Targeting Zero, and it was chaired by Professor Stephen Duckett at the Grattan
Institute who is in our Melbourne studio. Welcome Stephen.

Stephen Duckett: Good evening, Norman.

Norman Swan: So you did this review, it wasn't of the Djerriwarrh service
because that's already been done by the Safety and Quality Council and
Professor Euan Wallace. You were looking at the system in general.

Stephen Duckett: Yes, we were looking more broadly. Obviously the report was
stimulated, the inquiry was stimulated by the Djerriwarrh health service tragedy.
But we were looking at the overall system and the governance of the whole
system.

Norman Swan: And just to get the sense of this right, we are not…when things
go wrong, it's not usually because of a bad egg, is because the system goes
wrong. So we are not looking for a head on a stick here.

Stephen Duckett: No, there are quite separate processes, including the
Australian Health Professional Registration Authority that looks at those bad egg
issues. We were looking at the overall system governance, the processes, the
information and that sort of thing.

Norman Swan: So you weren't that kind to the Victorian Health Department.

Stephen Duckett: Well, we were quite strong in our language. There were these
11 potentially avoidable deaths, and this is a tragedy, and I would like to see that
we learnt from that.

Norman Swan: So what do you think the main learnings are from your review?

Stephen Duckett: Victoria is right at the forefront of being well regarded as the
most efficient state in terms of public hospital provision. But other states have

jumped ahead of Victoria in terms of quality and safety governance. New South
Wales has a much better infrastructure for governance of quality and safety
following the Garling Report I think a decade or so ago. Queensland, much better
systems of tracking and monitoring safety issues following the Patel Bundaberg
tragedy. South Australia, a better incident reporting system. So other states are
going ahead, and Victoria hasn't kept up with them.

Norman Swan: So what sort of changes are you suggesting?

Stephen Duckett: Well, we've got a number of them, there's 180 almost
recommendations. But some of them are these things where we want more
clinical engagement. The department wasn't using the skills, knowledge of
clinicians as much as it ought. We want more transparency, we want to be
publishing how hospitals are going, public and private in terms of their safety and
quality performance. And we want to have the health department being more
supportive of health services and providing advice. At the moment every single
hospital has to reinvent the safety and quality wheel, and there's not as much
sharing of knowledge and transmission of knowledge about what works across
the health system.

Norman Swan: Despite Victoria being proud of its system and its decentralised
approach, it is unique in that I think there are something like 85 different health
services in Victoria, whereas in New South Wales it might be…I don't know what
it is, 17, similar sort of number in Queensland. So they've shrunk it down from
bigger services. And I think one of your findings was that in Victoria you've got
some very small services which don't really have the skills to look after
themselves properly in terms of safety and quality.

Stephen Duckett: Yes, so we have proposed strengthening the boards. At the
moment some of these boards have been in place…the members have been on
them for 20 or 30 years, and so there's no turnover, no new ideas coming
through. There is not an adequate process for ensuring that they've got the right
skills. At the moment there is a tick box; do you have clinical governance skills or
not. Who knows what that means? And so we are proposing major strengthening
of the board level clinical governance because they are the ones that are legally
accountable.

Norman Swan: Let's talk about clinical governance because the average listener
listening to us now wouldn't have a clue what we are talking about. We are
talking about clinicians sitting around a table trying to look at events that might
have occurred in the hospital, then doing research into why that would happen so
it doesn't happen again. And just anecdotally, it depends on rather honest
conversations occurring which probably don't really occur. So you're talking
about engaging doctors more in this, but they are actually traditionally quite
scared to bring this up with their colleagues, even people who you would think
are just big bruiser orthopaedic surgeons and would be scared of anything, but
there are actually scared of raising stuff with their colleagues.

Stephen Duckett: Yes, there are two paths we are really talking about. One is
these events, the unusual, the sentinel events, as they're called, operating on the
wrong body part or leaving something in the wound. They are very unusual, and
they are investigated to death, in a sense. What we also need to be looking at is
patterns of care. To what extent are there more hospital-acquired infections in
your hospital, in your clinical unit, in your orthopaedic unit than in the state
average. And unfortunately what has happened in Victoria is the hospitals
themselves don't have enough information about what the state average is, they
even don't have good information about how they are tracking against their own
history. So by focusing on patterns, you…I won't say make the person irrelevant,
but it gets you to focus more on the systems, it gets you to focus on are there
systematic things happening in this hospital that aren't happening in other
hospitals.

Norman Swan: You also say in your report, which would shock the average
person, is that safety and quality doesn't have a high enough profile, either at a
state level or at a hospital level.

Stephen Duckett: Yes, as I said, Victoria is very proud of the fact that it's the
most efficient state in terms of the public hospital system, and they've
strengthened their emphasis on safety and quality in recent years. But the
example I use is there's a performance assessment scale that is used to rank
hospitals, to track how they are going. And at the moment there are three
dimensions to it. Are you going on budget? And that's worth 30% of the score…

Norman Swan: And the second one is are you going on budget, and the third
one is are you going on budget, is it?

Stephen Duckett: Not quite as bad as that, Norman! But the first one is are you
going on budget, the second one is how are you going on your waiting list, and
the third one is quality and safety. Originally that was only 15%, and they have
increased that to 40%.

But when I wait around Victoria and said to people; do you think it's the right idea
that if you go better on budget you are allowed to go worse on quality and
safety? I couldn't find anybody who thought that was a good idea at all. So quality
and safety…

Norman Swan: It's got to sit there in its own right.

Stephen Duckett: Yes, it ought to be there in its own right, it ought to be
something that we focus on, and it's not at the moment.

Norman Swan: But to do this you can't expect a single service, even a large
service like, say, Royal Melbourne or the Alfred, you can't expect them to do a lot
of this stuff by themselves. The department is going to have to do a lot for them,
aren't they?

Stephen Duckett: Yes, exactly. So what we are saying is there needs to be way
more support from the Department to these services, and so for example in New
South Wales there is a portal that clinicians across the state can access which
provides them with information about how they are tracking against their peers,
how they are tracking against the state average. We don't have that in Victoria.
And so we need to be providing more support to the clinicians in our hospitals,
big and small, to help them address these important issues.

Norman Swan: When there was a problem in Britain in a hospital in Staffordshire
in the Midlands, the big question in the National Health Service was how many
more Staffordshires are there. Do we know how many more Djerriwarrhs there
are in Victoria or indeed any other state in Australia?

Stephen Duckett: I think some states are better than others in tracking what's
going wrong, and in trying to identify the issues. When I was in Queensland, this

was one of the things…we wanted to err on identifying things early. And so we
probably over-investigated, just to make sure that Bundaberg would never
happen again, or reduce to a small risk that Bundaberg happen again. We
haven't had that same focus in Victoria, and I think that's what we need.

Norman Swan: And just finally Stephen, how much can other states learn
from…you say that other states are ahead of Victoria in some respects, but how
much is this applicable to other states?

Stephen Duckett: There are some national issues that we raise. So, for
example, there needs to be better sharing of information between the registration
regulation bodies and the health services, because we know that if a person, a
doctor for example, has complaints against him or her, they are more likely to
have complaints against them in the future. But we don't get that information, it's
secret squirrel business in the regulator. And so we need to have much more
sharing of information. So there are some national issues that we touch on in that
report.

Norman Swan: Thanks very much Stephen, and that's available on the Health
Department's website?

Stephen Duckett: On the Health Department website. Thanks very much
Norman.

Norman Swan: Stephen Duckett, who is head of the health program at the
Grattan Institute in Melbourne.

You're listening to the Health Report here on RN with me, Norman Swan.

There is a form of treatment for depression called behavioural activation. There's
just been a fascinating trial published in the Lancet comparing it to the standard
psychotherapy for depression called cognitive behavioural therapy. And one of
the authors of this trial is David Ekers from the University of Durham. Welcome to
the Health Report.

David Ekers: Hiya Norman.

Norman Swan: What is behavioural activation?

David Ekers: Behavioural activation, it's not a new treatment for depression, it's
been around a long time, and it has a view that depression is not necessarily
something wrong inside us but something that has happened that has cut us off
from those things in our world that are important or antidepressant to us. And as
that happens, if it happens to any of us we would feel down, it would affect our
mood, and sometimes when people feel down, to cope they tend to put things off
or shut down, and when they shut down they become further isolated from those
things, and thus the loop develops.

So behavioural activation is a relatively simple treatment that aims at helping
people understand that relationship between what they do and how they feel, and
then look at changing what they do on a day-to-day basis, just with small gradual
steps to put them back in touch with the things in their world that are healthy and
antidepressants to them, and in that way subsequently they change how they
feel. So we call that in BA working from the outside in.

Norman Swan: So what did you used to enjoy, doing kind of an audit of things
you used to have fun with and that you are not doing now.

David Ekers: Yes, it's a little bit more complicated than just fun. It would be
lovely to think we could live a hedonistic lifestyle…

Norman Swan: Yes, particularly going to the football if your team is not winning,
yes.

David Ekers: Yes, it's things that are valuable, that give us a sense of purpose or
meaning in our day-to-day lives. Some of that will be pleasure, some of it will be
necessary tasks, some of it will be things like going to work or communicating
with family members. Not all of it is pleasurable but it's functional for us. So BA is
a contextual treatment, it looks at depression as sat in the context of your life.

Norman Swan: So I take it that the activation piece is not 'get up off your arse
and stop feeling sorry to yourself'.

David Ekers: No, not at all. What BA does is first of all it explores that concept
with people. So it develops…

Norman Swan: So you understand what the meaning of those activities were.

David Ekers: Yes, and then you understand how they have gone out of your life.
Because they go out of your life often for a reason. Things will have happened
that will make it difficult to do those things, so we explore that with somebody,
then we get them to look at the relationship at the moment between what they
are doing and how they're feeling, and then we gradually work together to
develop a plan, a thing called activity scheduling, to put people back in touch with
that stuff. And then you regularly monitor that and you look at blocks in that
treatment and work out what people can do to get out of…

Norman Swan: So there's a bit of cognitive stuff in there as well. You might
think, well, I can't go and do that because everybody knows I've been depressed
and they're going to think that I'm weak and hopeless. And you've got to get
beyond that negative thought as well.

David Ekers: Yes, but it's fundamentally different to cognitive behavioural
therapy. So in behavioural activation what we do is we are more interested in the
consequence of thinking that way. So we will recognise how people ruminate and
think about things, we all do that and it's much, much worse if we are
experiencing depression. We get less into trying to challenge the meaning of that
for an individual, which is how cognitive behavioural therapy works, and we are
much more interested in the consequence of that. So when you started feeling
that way, what did you do? And when you did that, how did you feel? And was
that in the longer term more beneficial? In the short term people do things to take
away the stress, but in the longer term we look at how that keeps people where
they are.

Norman Swan: I spent so long talking about behavioural activation, I'm almost
running out of time here to talk about your trial, but essentially you did a semi-
randomised trial of comparing behavioural activation with quite inexperienced
therapists, in other words, they weren't PhDs in psychology, versus a course of
cognitive behavioural therapy. What did you find?

David Ekers: Well, it was a randomised trial, it was a completely randomised
trial. Participants were randomised completely at random away from the
control…

Norman Swan: Oh I thought you selected people to make sure that you had a
balanced set of…

David Ekers: No, we made sure each group were balanced on a few things,
which is good quality randomised controlled trial. And what we found was non-
inferiority. So we found that BA delivered by non-specialists was not inferior in
any way to the current goal standard of CBT delivered by therapists…

Norman Swan: So does non-inferior mean just as good as?

David Ekers: Well, not quite. What you do is you set an inferiority margin around
on a measure and you would plan to get your new treatment, the BA, within that
margin of the gold standard, because to prove something is exactly the same
you'd need an unfeasibly large study to do that.

Norman Swan: And you found it was also significantly cheaper?

David Ekers: Yes, we got about a 20% reduction in costs. So I think what is
interesting in this study, the National Institute for Clinical Excellence over here
asked for this study to be done, but what's really interesting is what we've shown
is that a very effective psychological treatment can be delivered by non-
specialists to the same standards as specialists. And when we have difficulty in
access to psychological treatments, which I think is worldwide, this could offer
some promise.

Norman Swan: Dr David Ekers, who is clinical senior lecturer in the School of
Medicine, Pharmacy and Health in Durham University in the UK.

I'm Norman Swan, this has been the Health Report, and I'll see you next week.
